video.title: Why Are There Eyes All Over The Wheels In Ezekiel's Vision?
video.description:
A priest who has lost his temple. A throne on wheels. And rims covered in eyes, all looking back at him.

In 593 BC, Ezekiel is an exile by the Chebar canal in Babylon, far from the temple where he was meant to serve. Then the heavens open. The strangest vision in the Old Testament follows, with four-faced living creatures, wheels within wheels, and rims "full of eyes."

But what are the eyes for? This video follows the question through Ezekiel's book. It begins with a sentence the elders of Jerusalem were whispering in the dark, then traces the glory of God as it slowly leaves the temple. It ends with the detail that changes how you read the whole vision: the throne was already in Babylon.

What you'll discover:

Why Ezekiel's priestly calling makes the timing of this vision so striking
The whispered words of Jerusalem's elders, and how the wheels may answer them
The man in linen with a writing kit, and the mark on the foreheads of those who grieve
Why the departure of God's glory is described so slowly
What the order of the visions reveals about where the throne went
How Zechariah, Revelation, and the Lamb with seven eyes connect to the same image

Key Scripture in this video

The vision

Ezekiel 1:1-3: the date, the opened heavens, and the hand of the Lord
Ezekiel 1:4-14: the storm, the fire, and the four living creatures
Ezekiel 1:15-21: the wheels, the rims "full of eyes," and the spirit in the wheels
Ezekiel 1:22-28: the crystal expanse, the sapphire throne, and "the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord"

The whisper in Jerusalem

Ezekiel 8:3-18: the Spirit lifts Ezekiel by a lock of his hair, and he sees the idol, the hidden chamber, Tammuz, and sun worship
Ezekiel 8:12 and 9:9: "The Lord does not see us, the Lord has forsaken the land"

Mercy and judgment

Ezekiel 9:1-6: the six executioners, the man in linen, and the mark on those who sigh and groan
Ezekiel 10:12: the cherubim's whole bodies "full of eyes"

The glory departs

Ezekiel 10:18-19: the glory moves from the threshold to the east gate
Ezekiel 11:22-23: the glory rises and stands on the mountain east of the city
Ezekiel 10:15, 10:20: "the same living creatures I had seen by the River Chebar"
Ezekiel 11:16: "I have been a sanctuary to them for a little while" in the lands where they had gone

The eyes across Scripture

2 Chronicles 16:9
Proverbs 15:3
Zechariah 4:10
Revelation 4:6-8 and 5:6: the living creatures full of eyes, and the Lamb with seven eyes, "the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth"

The return

Ezekiel 43:1-5: the glory returns from the east, "like the vision I had seen by the River Chebar"
Ezekiel 48:35: "The Lord Is There"

Note on interpretation: This video separates what Scripture states from what it suggests. Connecting the eyes to the elders' whisper is an interpretation, since the text never says it outright. The link to Babylonian guardian figures is a scholarly theory. The alternative reading of the Hebrew word ayin (eye, or gleam) is also discussed.



💬 Question for you: Which part of Ezekiel's vision stayed with you the most? Tell me in the comments.

🔔 Subscribe for more Bible mysteries explored one passage at a time.

transcript.text: The wheel is standing on the ground, and Ezekiel is close enough to see the rim. The rim is looking back at him.
Eyes set into the curve of the wheel, one after another all the way around.
A handful would have been strange enough, but scripture says the rims were full of them.
The year is 593 BC. The place is a canal in Babylon, far from home.
And the man staring at the wheel is a priest who has not served in a temple for years.
Why would the throne of God roll on wheels covered with eyes?
Readers have argued about that question for 26 centuries.
But hundreds of miles away in Jerusalem, a group of elders was whispering a sentence in the dark.
And Ezekiel will hear it soon. When he does, he will understand that every one of those eyes was an answer to it.
Ezekiel opens his book with a date.
It is the fifth day of the fourth month, in the fifth year of the exile of king Jehoiachin.
Ezekiel is among the Judeans dragged to Babylon four years earlier, and he is living beside the River Chebar, a canal cut through the Babylonian plain.
The first verse also says that the heavens were opened.
Most of what happens in the chapter comes in a sentence the prophet has no way to prepare for.
The hand of the Lord was upon him there, there in Babylon, which was the last place any exile expected God to show up.
Then the storm arrives.
Ezekiel sees a windstorm out of the north, a vast cloud with fire flashing inside it, and a glow at its center like gleaming metal.
Out of the fire come four living creatures.
Each has four faces, those of a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle.
Each has four wings and human hands beneath the wings.
Fire moves between them like torches, and the creatures dart back and forth like lightning.
Then comes the part the chapter is famous for.
Beside each creature is a wheel, a wheel that looks as though another wheel is cutting straight through it.
The wheels gleam like beryl.
They can travel in any of four directions without ever turning.
And the rims are high, and they are awesome, and they are full of eyes.
Above the creatures spreads a surface like shining crystal.
Above that is a throne the color of sapphire.
On the throne sits a figure like a man, wrapped in fire and surrounded by a brightness Ezekiel compares to a rainbow in the clouds.
The prophet closes the scene with a sentence of careful restraint.
This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord.
Notice the layers of hedging, appearance of the likeness of the glory.
Ezekiel is reaching for words that do not exist.
When it ends, he does what a man should do.
He falls on his face.
Hold that image for a moment, because the vision hides something that most people read straight past.
We will come back to it.
Ezekiel was a priest, and scripture says he was 30 when this happened.
That detail matters, because in Israel 30 was the age a priest began his service at the temple.
Many interpreters, including some of the early church writers, understand the 30th year this way.
If so, this was the very year Ezekiel should have been standing at an altar in Jerusalem.
Instead, he was sitting beside a canal in a pagan empire, and the career he trained for had been taken from him.
Picture a man in that position, the way you would if you were told the thing you were born for had been canceled.
He is cut off from the temple, and he has no reason to believe heaven even knows where he is.
That is the moment the sky opens.
This opening is where I have to pause for a moment.
Everything you will hear in this video rests on one belief about the unseen realm, that it is real, that it is awake, and that it is paying attention.
Before we ask what the eyes mean, we have to ask who Ezekiel's vision was meant for.
The exiles had a theology, and it was a comfortable one.
God lived in the temple, the temple stood in Jerusalem, and Jerusalem would never fall.
They had been carried off to Babylon, but they were telling themselves it was temporary.
The temple still stood, God was still home.
They were the ones who had been misplaced.
Chapter 1 shatters that picture without a word of argument.
The throne of God turns up in Babylon on wheels.

transcript.text: Think about what that order means.
When the glory finally lifted off the threshold in Jerusalem, where did it go?
The text does not spell out the destination, but Ezekiel recognizes the vehicle at once.
In chapter 10, he says plainly that these were the living creatures he had seen by the river Chebar.
The chariot that rose from the temple was the same one he had already met in Babylon.
In other words, the throne was never trapped in a building.
Jerusalem's idolaters could not lock heaven in, and the enemy could not bar it out.
Now, the design of the wheels starts to make sense.
A throne with wheels is a throne that can move.
Wheels that go in four directions without turning, mean the throne never has to face away from any part of the earth.
And the eyes ringed all around the rims mean it can see in every direction at once.
Taken together, these details describe a god who cannot be left behind, who cannot be hidden from, and who cannot be confined to one place.
Scripture then adds one more detail that I think is the quiet center of the passage.
In chapter 1, we are told that the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.
The wheels are not dead machinery, they move because the spirit moves them.
Zechariah later writes that the eyes of the Lord range through the whole earth, and the book of Revelation will go further and connect the eyes to the spirit directly.
Taken together, the passages suggest that the eyes and the wheels are tied to the spirit of God, ranging, watching, present.
And then the Lord says to Ezekiel something that the exiles had never dared to hope for.

In chapter 11, speaking about the very people who had been cast out, he says that although he had sent them far away among the nations, he would be a sanctuary to them for a little while in the countries where they had gone.
A sanctuary in Babylon.
There is one further piece of context.
Scholars note that Babylon was filled with winged guardian figures, human-headed bulls and lions standing at the gates of palaces and temples.
That is a theory, and it is only a theory.
But if it is right, then the exiles looked at the creatures in Ezekiel's vision and recognized something from the imperial culture around them.
And they would have seen that the real throne was held up by living things far greater than anything Babylon had carved in stone.
God was borrowing the images of their captors and showing that the true power sat elsewhere.
The elders in Jerusalem thought the Lord could not see them, the exiles in Babylon thought he could not reach them.
The vision answers both at once.
Ezekiel's book does not end at the departure of the glory.
It ends in a return.
In chapter 43, Ezekiel is brought to the east gate of a new temple, and he sees the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east.
The sound is like many waters, the earth shines with his glory.
And Ezekiel says that the vision was like the one he had seen by the river Chebar.
The same chariot, the same wheels, the same presence that left the old temple comes back through the east, retracing the path it took when it left.
And the book's final sentence gives the city a new name.
The name of the city from that day on will be, The Lord is There.
So what was the mystery of the eyes?
On the surface, the answer is simple.
They tell us that God sees.
But the details of Ezekiel's vision carry that idea much further than most people read it.
God sees the hidden rooms and the secret shrines.

transcript.text: God sees the hidden rooms and the secret shrines, and nothing is invisible to him.
But he also sees the grief of a priest by a canal, and the sighing of a faithful few in a doomed city.
And he marks them. The eyes that terrified the guilty were the same eyes that kept the faithful from being forgotten.
Centuries later, John would stand on another island of exile, and write down his own vision.
He would see living creatures full of eyes in front and behind, and he would see the lamb with seven eyes,
which John says are the seven spirits of God, sent out into all the earth.
It is the same gaze, now carried by the lamb who was slain.
The watching God does not only record the world's sorrow, he steps into it.
And that, I think, is why the opening image of the story lands the way it does.
Ezekiel was a man who thought heaven had lost track of him.
He had a canal, an empire, and a ruined calling.
Then a wheel rolled up beside him, and its rim opened its eyes and looked at him.
The mystery was never really about the wheels. It was about a question every exile eventually asks:
the question of whether anyone sees.
Ezekiel's answer came in the form of a throne that no army could capture, and no distance could outrun.
Wherever you are tonight, in whatever Babylon you have landed in, the God of the wheels has not lost sight of you.
What part of Ezekiel's vision stayed with you the most?
Tell me in the comments, and if this opened up the passage in a new way, subscribe,
because there is more of Scripture waiting to be read this closely.
